## Abstract {#abstract}

This tutorial provides a practical workflow for specifying scalar variance-component priors in Bayesian multilevel models. It reviews gamma, inverse-gamma, half-*t*, and half-Cauchy priors and clarifies how prior meaning changes across variance, precision, and standard-deviation parameterizations. A worked TIMSS 2019 example uses benchmark information from a non-overlapping reference sample to construct alternative priors for a smaller target analysis. The emphasis is on making the rationale, translation, checking, and robustness of prior choices visible rather than treating any default as automatically neutral.

## Practical Workflow {#workflow}

::: {.workflow-list}
<div><span>01</span><strong>Identify the target variance component and implementation scale.</strong><p>Clarify whether the software expects a variance, precision, standard deviation, or transformed parameter.</p></div>
<div><span>02</span><strong>Choose benchmark values and prior informativeness.</strong><p>Use substantive knowledge, prior studies, historical data, or a clearly separated reference sample when appropriate.</p></div>
<div><span>03</span><strong>Calibrate a prior family on an interpretable scale.</strong><p>Relate plausible parameter magnitudes to gamma, inverse-gamma, half-t, or half-Cauchy hyperparameters.</p></div>
<div><span>04</span><strong>Translate the prior into the estimation environment.</strong><p>Check the software parameterization before carrying numerical hyperparameters across programs.</p></div>
<div><span>05</span><strong>Inspect and stress-test the prior.</strong><p>Use density inspection, prior predictive checking, posterior comparison, convergence assessment, and sensitivity analysis.</p></div>
<div><span>06</span><strong>Report the rationale and robustness checks.</strong><p>Document the parameter scale, prior family, hyperparameters, source of benchmark information, and sensitivity results.</p></div>
:::

## Practical Safeguards {#practical-safeguards}

::: {.mini-grid}
<div><strong>Prior-density inspection</strong><br><span>Check where mass is concentrated before fitting the target model.</span></div>
<div><strong>Prior predictive checks</strong><br><span>Ask whether the prior implies plausible data-generating behavior.</span></div>
<div><strong>Posterior comparison</strong><br><span>Compare conclusions under alternative defensible specifications.</span></div>
<div><strong>Transparent reporting</strong><br><span>Make the prior reconstructable by another analyst.</span></div>
:::

## Key Takeaways

- A numerical prior specification is not portable unless the **parameter scale and software parameterization** are also understood.
- Benchmark-informed calibration is most defensible when the source of information and its separation from the target analysis are explicit.
- Sensitivity analysis is part of prior specification, not a final cosmetic check.
- The goal is not to identify one universal prior family, but to make prior assumptions interpretable, inspectable, and reproducible.

## Contribution to my research program

This tutorial is the translational component of my Bayesian methods program. It turns simulation-based findings on prior performance into an applied workflow researchers can use when moving across models, prior families, parameterizations, and software environments.
